task_brief: Day 2 of "Cybersecurity Foundations in a Sandbox" (unit 5, grade 10) is a worked-model trace on authentication and authorization concepts. It is one step inside the unit — not the whole unit project — and takes about 45–75 minutes. The unit is working toward: Write a threat model and defensive hardening plan for a fictional system inside a sandbox; no live or third-party system is probed. Today's work contributes to that by handling authentication and authorization concepts at the explicit model stage, against the unit's wider topics of confidentiality integrity and availability, authentication and authorization concepts, encryption and hashing concepts, and recognising and defending against common vulnerability classes. This session is formative: it is scored on completeness and honesty of the record, not on getting a polished result.
primary_task: Work through the provided worked model of authentication and authorization concepts one step at a time rather than reading it straight through. For each step, write what changed and why that step is legal. Build a trace table with one row per step showing the values or states before and after. Then change exactly one line, value, or condition in the model, predict the new result before running or re-tracing it, and record whether your prediction was right. Explain in your own words the rule that makes authentication and authorization concepts behave the way the model shows. Anchor today's work inside its unit: this session's evidence is about authentication and authorization concepts, and it belongs to "Cybersecurity Foundations in a Sandbox", which also covers separate topics such as confidentiality integrity and availability. Close out with this check before you stop: Explain the modelled approach to authentication and authorization concepts in your own words and name the step most likely to go wrong. At grade 10 the bar is independent work that justifies its approach against a named alternative you considered and rejected, with the trade-off stated concretely.

presentation_and_privacy.sandbox_and_credentials_note: Everything in this task runs in a sandbox or on paper. Never use a real password, passphrase, API key, account credential, access token, precise home location, or any real person's identifiable information — invent fictional values instead. Do not sign into, probe, scan, stress, or attempt access to any live, production, school, or third-party system, and do not bypass a filter, licence, access control, or terms of service. Any practice login used in an example must be obviously invented — a silly made-up name paired with a nonsense multi-word phrase — and must never be anything you or anyone in your family actually uses somewhere real. If a task seems to need something real, substitute a made-up stand-in and note the substitution.

copyright_and_authorship: The graded submission must be your own authorship. A parent, tutor, or AI tool may explain an idea, demonstrate a technique, or give feedback on a draft, but must not produce, write, debug, or make any part of the work that is scored. Any code, asset, or text you did not write must be openly licensed or supplied for this task, and must be cited in a comment or note naming where it came from and what you changed.
accessibility_options: Provide readable text plus optional audio or read-aloud support; no voice feature is required.
Chunk directions into one action at a time and show a worked example or model.
Offer reduced-copying, extended-time, hidden-timer, movement-break, and low-distraction options.
Use captions, alt text, high-contrast print, keyboard access, and text-only fallbacks for media.
For any multi-session project, supply a written milestone plan, checkpoint dates, and a task breakdown, so executive-function load is not silently part of what is being assessed.

Adjust quantity, pacing, representation, or response mode while holding the target constant. Where the target names a specific skill, change how it is evidenced rather than substituting a different skill.
Accept typed, handwritten, spoken, diagrammed, or demonstrated responses; where code is the target, accept pseudocode, block-based, or annotated-trace evidence.
Provide screen-reader-compatible editors, adjustable font and contrast, keyboard-only workflows, and an offline paper-and-trace route for every programming task.
task_accessibility_provisions: Provide a screen-reader-compatible editor, adjustable font size and contrast, and a complete keyboard-only workflow. An offline paper-and-trace route is available for every task here and is scored identically to an on-screen one.

Any model, source, or artifact under study is supplied in an accessible parallel form: text alternative or transcript, described version, and a tactile or enlarged rendering where the original is visual. The learner is never required to perceive the source in one specific channel to analyse it.
Breaks, extended time, a hidden timer, reduced copying, and a low-distraction setting are available on request and never reduce the score.
safety_and_privacy_rules: Allow a pause, break, or alternate response mode without treating it as failure.
Never use or require a real password, API key, access token, account credential, private message, precise location, or identifiable image; use clearly fictional placeholder values only.
Keep all security work in sandboxed, simulated, or fictional environments; never scan, probe, exploit, or attempt access against real systems, networks, accounts, services, or people.
Use approved sites and tools; do not bypass filters, access controls, licensing, or terms of service.
Treat AI output as a draft to verify and disclose. The tutor may explain concepts, ask diagnostic questions, and help debug, but never silently completes graded project work.

remediation: Reteaching for authentication and authorization concepts follows the signal actually observed, not a fixed script. If the signal is "prerequisite gap": Return to the smallest prerequisite needed for authentication and authorization concepts, model it in a concrete or text-only representation, then retry one fresh item. If the signal is "procedure without understanding": Ask the learner to explain or represent why the approach to authentication and authorization concepts works before continuing. If the signal is "correct but low confidence": Confirm the reasoning specifically, offer one varied example of authentication and authorization concepts, and avoid unnecessary remediation. If the signal is "repeated error pattern": Name the observable pattern neutrally, contrast it with a worked example, and schedule a short same-day or next-session review. If the signal is "requests the answer to graded work": Explain the concept, ask a diagnostic question, or help isolate the defect. Do not supply the graded artifact, solution code, or finished creative work. If the signal is "mastery evidence": Require accurate independent application plus explanation on a later or different occasion before marking authentication and authorization concepts mastered. Re-check with one fresh item of the same kind before moving on, and record which signal was seen so the pattern is visible across the unit rather than treated as a one-off.
extension: Apply authentication and authorization concepts under a new constraint, compare two approaches or perspectives, or explain the idea to someone else using an original example. Treat this as optional depth on authentication and authorization concepts rather than extra volume: one harder case done well beats three more of the same. Extension work stays inside the same sandbox rules — no real credentials and no live external systems. Extension work is never required to reach mastery and must not be assigned as a penalty.
